title: A pedestrian approaches the zebra crossing
brief: Town road, 40 km/h, light traffic. A zebra crossing is ahead.
question: What is the safest response?

choices.t: Slow down and stop before the crossing to let them cross.
choices.why: A pedestrian stepping onto a zebra crossing has priority. Slowing early lets you stop smoothly before the stop line.

choices.t: Sound the horn and continue — they will wait.
choices.why: The horn is a warning, not a right of way. The pedestrian may step out anyway, and you are legally required to give way at a zebra crossing.

choices.t: Speed up to pass before they reach your lane.
choices.why: Accelerating towards a crossing removes your margin. If they keep walking, you hit them at a higher speed.

choices.t: Swerve into the right lane to go around them.
choices.why: Swerving puts you into oncoming traffic and still crosses the pedestrian's path.

title: The car ahead brakes hard
brief: Two-lane road, 60 km/h. You are following a car.
question: The brake lights come on suddenly. What do you do?

choices.t: Brake firmly and progressively, keeping straight in your lane.
choices.why: Braking in a straight line uses all your tyres' grip for stopping. With a three-second gap you have room to do it smoothly.

choices.t: Swerve right to go past.
choices.why: A lorry is coming the other way. Swerving into the oncoming lane turns a rear-end risk into a head-on one.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep your speed.
choices.why: The horn does not stop you. You will close the gap at full speed.

choices.t: Pull the parking brake hard.
choices.why: The foot brake is far more powerful and stable; yanking the parking brake can lock the rear wheels and spin the car.

title: A motorcycle in your blind spot
brief: Divided city road, two lanes your way. You want to move to the right lane.
question: You have checked your mirror and signalled right. What next?

choices.t: Look over your right shoulder, see the motorcycle, and wait until it has passed.
choices.why: Two-wheelers easily hide in the blind spot beside your rear pillar. The shoulder check is what finds them.

choices.t: Move across — your indicator is on.
choices.why: A signal is information, not permission. The rider may not have seen it, and you would cut across their path.

choices.t: Brake hard and stay where you are.
choices.why: Hard braking without need risks a rear-end crash. Hold your speed and simply wait for the gap.

choices.t: Accelerate hard and change lanes ahead of it.
choices.why: Racing a vehicle you have not properly seen is guesswork, and it closes up on the bus ahead.

title: Cattle near the road at dusk
brief: Rural road at dusk, 50 km/h. A cow is grazing at the right edge.
question: The cow starts drifting towards the road. What do you do?

choices.t: Ease off, brake gently and be ready to stop; do not swerve sharply.
choices.why: Animals move unpredictably. Slowing early keeps every option open; a sharp swerve can roll a car or send it into a ditch or oncoming traffic.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep going — it will move away.
choices.why: A frightened animal may run in any direction, including into your path.

choices.t: Swerve hard left onto the shoulder.
choices.why: Violent steering at speed can cause a loss of control, especially on a rough shoulder.

choices.t: Flash high beam to scare it.
choices.why: Bright light can freeze or confuse animals rather than move them.

title: A car edges out of a side road
brief: Main road, 50 km/h. A side road joins from the left.
question: The car's nose creeps past the give-way line. What do you do?

choices.t: Ease off, cover the brake and be ready to stop — assume they may pull out.
choices.why: A car creeping forward may not have seen you. Being ready to stop costs a second; being wrong costs a crash.

choices.t: Continue — you have priority on the main road.
choices.why: Priority is given, not taken. Plenty of side-impact crashes involve a driver who was legally in the right.

choices.t: Speed up to get past before they move.
choices.why: If they pull out, you will hit them harder and have less time to brake.

choices.t: Move into the oncoming lane to give them space.
choices.why: You cannot see what is coming the other way, and a sudden lane change surprises everyone.

title: A car suddenly changes lanes in front of you
brief: Divided highway, 80 km/h. A car is in the right lane slightly ahead.
question: It swings into your lane without signalling. What do you do?

choices.t: Ease off and brake gently to rebuild a safe gap.
choices.why: Opening the gap restores your stopping margin. Their mistake does not need to become your crash.

choices.t: Sound the horn and hold your speed to make a point.
choices.why: Holding speed keeps you too close. Showing them their mistake does not make you any safer.

choices.t: Accelerate and overtake them on the left.
choices.why: Overtaking on the left is unsafe and illegal, and angry overtakes are how road rage starts.

choices.t: Swerve onto the shoulder.
choices.why: A sudden swerve at 80 km/h is more dangerous than braking, and the shoulder may hold stopped vehicles or people.

title: Children at a school gate
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. School is just finishing; children are at the gate beside a crossing.
question: A child leaves the group near the kerb. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep your speed — they are on the footpath, not the road.
choices.why: A child can be in front of you in a second; being on the footpath now means nothing.

choices.t: Sound the horn continuously as you pass.
choices.why: The horn can startle a child into running the wrong way, and it does not slow you down.

choices.t: Slow right down and be ready to stop — children can dart out without looking.
choices.why: Children judge speed and distance poorly and act on impulse; low speed gives you time to stop.

choices.t: Overtake the car ahead to get past the school quickly.
choices.why: Overtaking near a school puts you closer to the kerb side children at higher speed.

title: A ball rolls into the road
brief: Residential street, 30 km/h, cars parked along the left.
question: A ball bounces out from between parked cars. What should you expect?

choices.t: Nothing — steer around the ball and carry on.
choices.why: The ball is rarely the danger; the child chasing it is.

choices.t: Speed up to clear the area before anyone appears.
choices.why: Speeding up cuts the time you have to react if a child steps out.

choices.t: A child may run out after it — brake now and be ready to stop.
choices.why: Where a ball goes, a child often follows without looking. Treat the ball as a warning.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep your speed.
choices.why: A child focused on a ball may not react to the horn at all.

title: A pedestrian looking at a phone
brief: Busy town road, 40 km/h. A man walks along the kerb, eyes on his phone.
question: He drifts towards the road edge. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep going — pedestrians must look before stepping out.
choices.why: Being right does not stop a collision. Drivers have to allow for others' mistakes.

choices.t: Slow down and move out a little if it's clear — he may step off without looking.
choices.why: Someone absorbed in a phone has not seen you. Space and lower speed cover their mistake.

choices.t: Brake hard to a stop in the lane.
choices.why: An unnecessary emergency stop risks a rear-end crash; easing off early is enough.

choices.t: Pass as close as possible to the centre line at the same speed.
choices.why: Moving out without slowing can bring you into oncoming traffic and still leaves little margin.

title: An elderly person on the crossing
brief: Town road, 30 km/h. An elderly woman is crossing slowly from the right.
question: Traffic behind you is impatient. What do you do?

choices.t: Drive behind her once she has passed the centre line.
choices.why: She is still crossing your lane; she might hesitate or step back.

choices.t: Sound the horn gently so she hurries.
choices.why: Hurrying someone unsteady on their feet makes a fall more likely.

choices.t: Wave her across and then move off immediately.
choices.why: Moving off before she reaches the kerb leaves no margin if she slows.

choices.t: Stop before the line and wait until she has fully crossed — don't edge forward or hoot.
choices.why: Older pedestrians need more time and may stop or turn back. Pressure from you can make them stumble.

title: Running for the bus
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. A bus has stopped on the other side.
question: A man on your left starts running towards the bus. What do you do?

choices.t: Hold your speed — the bus is on the other side, not yours.
choices.why: To reach the bus he has to cross your lane first.

choices.t: Speed up to pass before he reaches the road.
choices.why: You arrive sooner and faster — the worst combination if he runs out.

choices.t: Slow down and be ready to stop — he is likely to dash across without looking.
choices.why: People rushing for a bus look at the bus, not the traffic.

choices.t: Move right towards the bus to give him room on the left.
choices.why: You would drive towards the bus and the people around it.

title: Someone crossing a highway
brief: Four-lane highway, 70 km/h, you are in the left lane. A man stands in a gap in the median.
question: He steps off the median into your carriageway. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep going — pedestrians should not be on a highway.
choices.why: They often are; a collision at highway speed is rarely survivable.

choices.t: Brake firmly and check your mirror — he is likely to keep walking across both lanes into your path.
choices.why: People often cross highways at median gaps and misjudge fast traffic.

choices.t: Swerve right into the other lane without checking.
choices.why: A vehicle may be overtaking you in the right lane — and he is walking into it.

choices.t: Flash your lights and hold your speed.
choices.why: Flashing does not stop you, and he may freeze in your path.

title: Road works ahead
brief: Main road, 50 km/h. Workers are repairing the road; one stands in your lane with a red flag.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Keep going slowly around the worker on the right.
choices.why: You would drive into the oncoming lane without being waved through.

choices.t: Sound the horn so the worker moves aside.
choices.why: The worker is there to stop traffic; the horn changes nothing.

choices.t: Slow down early and follow the flag signal; stop if shown.
choices.why: A worker controlling traffic has to be obeyed, and workers may step back without looking.

choices.t: Speed up before the worker raises the flag.
choices.why: Rushing a work zone is how workers get hurt.

title: A procession on the road at night
brief: Town road at night, 30 km/h. A temple procession is walking in your lane.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Use the horn and lights to make them move aside.
choices.why: It can cause panic in a crowd and does not create a safe gap.

choices.t: Overtake on the right at normal speed.
choices.why: You cannot see who may step out from the group or oncoming traffic.

choices.t: Slow to walking pace and follow at a distance, or wait; pass only when there is clear room.
choices.why: Crowds spread unpredictably and people may not see you in the dark.

choices.t: Follow closely so they know you want to pass.
choices.why: Close following leaves no room if someone stops or falls.

title: An auto-rickshaw near a median gap
brief: City road, 40 km/h. An auto-rickshaw ahead slows near a gap in the centre.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Overtake it on the left while it slows.
choices.why: If it swings left first to make a U-turn, you are in its path.

choices.t: Overtake on the right before it turns.
choices.why: Passing on the side it is about to turn towards is the classic crash.

choices.t: Hold back and slow down — it may U-turn or stop without signalling.
choices.why: Autos often turn or stop suddenly for passengers or gaps; give them room and time.

choices.t: Follow closely so it cannot cut across.
choices.why: Following closely gives you no time to react to its next move.

title: An auto stops for a passenger
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. An auto-rickshaw is just ahead; someone waves from the kerb.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Ease off and leave room — it will probably pull over and stop sharply.
choices.why: A waving passenger is a strong clue the auto will stop or swerve to the kerb.

choices.t: Close up so you can pass the moment it stops.
choices.why: Too close and you have no space if it stops in the lane.

choices.t: Overtake on the left between the auto and the kerb.
choices.why: That is exactly where it is heading — and where the passenger is.

choices.t: Sound the horn so the driver doesn't stop.
choices.why: The driver will stop anyway; you need the gap, not the horn.

title: Turning left with bikes around
brief: Town junction, slowing to 15 km/h to turn left into the side road.
question: What do you check before turning?

choices.t: Only the right mirror for traffic behind.
choices.why: The danger in a left turn is on your left.

choices.t: Nothing — your indicator is on, so others will wait.
choices.why: An indicator tells others what you plan; it does not make the space clear.

choices.t: Left mirror and a look over your left shoulder — a bike may be filtering up your left side.
choices.why: Two-wheelers often pass on the left in slow traffic and sit right in your blind spot.

choices.t: Cut the corner quickly to get ahead of any bikes.
choices.why: Cutting the corner sweeps across the path of anything on your left.

title: A motorcycle on the wrong side
brief: Two-lane road, 40 km/h. A motorcycle is coming towards you in your lane, close to the edge.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Move to the centre line to show you have priority.
choices.why: Pushing out risks the oncoming lane and leaves the rider nowhere to go.

choices.t: Slow down, keep a steady line and give it room — expect it to stay on your side.
choices.why: Wrong-side riders rarely move across; predictable, slower movement from you helps both of you.

choices.t: Swerve onto the footpath.
choices.why: You might hit pedestrians or lose control on the kerb.

choices.t: Speed up and pass it quickly.
choices.why: A head-on encounter at higher speed is far more dangerous.

title: A cyclist wobbling ahead
brief: Two-lane road, 40 km/h. A cyclist with a heavy load wobbles near the edge; a car is coming the other way.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Squeeze past now between the cyclist and the oncoming car.
choices.why: No room for a wobble — a small swerve and you hit the cyclist or the car.

choices.t: Sound the horn so the cyclist moves further left.
choices.why: A startled, loaded cyclist may wobble even more or fall.

choices.t: Wait behind until the oncoming car has passed, then overtake with a wide gap.
choices.why: A loaded cyclist can swerve without warning; you need space on both sides, which you don't have yet.

choices.t: Follow very close until you can pass.
choices.why: If the cyclist falls, you need room to stop.

title: Passing parked cars
brief: Narrow town road, 30 km/h, a row of parked cars on your left.
question: You notice someone in the driver's seat of a parked car. What do you do?

choices.t: Pass as close to the parked cars as possible to stay away from the centre line.
choices.why: Staying tight to parked cars puts you exactly where a door opens.

choices.t: Sound the horn as you pass every parked car.
choices.why: Constant horn use doesn't create space and annoys everyone.

choices.t: Speed past before the door can open.
choices.why: You can't outrun a door; speed only makes the impact worse.

choices.t: Slow down and leave about a door's width — the door may open or they may step out.
choices.why: Someone inside a parked car is a clue that a door could swing open into your path.

title: Pulling in to the left
brief: Busy city road, 30 km/h in slow traffic. You want to pull in to the kerb on your left to stop.
question: What must you do before moving left?

choices.t: Indicate and move across in one smooth movement.
choices.why: Indicating doesn't clear the space — a bike may already be there.

choices.t: Check the left mirror and look over your left shoulder — a motorcycle may be coming up on your left.
choices.why: Two-wheelers often pass on the left; your mirror alone can miss them.

choices.t: Check only your interior mirror.
choices.why: The interior mirror doesn't show the space beside you.

choices.t: Move left slowly so anyone there can get out of the way.
choices.why: Drifting into an occupied space forces a rider to brake or crash.

title: A rider ahead and a pothole
brief: Town road after rain, 40 km/h. A motorcycle is ahead; there is a large pothole in front of it.
question: What should you expect?

choices.t: The rider will swerve around the pothole — hold back and leave room on both sides.
choices.why: Riders steer around potholes at the last moment, often towards the centre of the lane.

choices.t: Nothing — overtake now while the rider is close to the edge.
choices.why: You'd be alongside exactly when the rider swerves out.

choices.t: The rider will brake — so close up and wait.
choices.why: Closing up removes your space whichever way the rider moves.

choices.t: Sound the horn to stop the rider moving out.
choices.why: The rider still has to avoid the pothole; the horn can cause a wobble.

title: A group of riders weaving
brief: Four-lane road, 50 km/h. A group of young riders is weaving between both lanes ahead.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Overtake them as fast as you can.
choices.why: You'd be alongside riders who can cut across at any moment.

choices.t: Use the horn repeatedly to break up the group.
choices.why: It can provoke or startle them into a fall.

choices.t: Drop back, keep a large gap and don't try to pass until they settle into one lane.
choices.why: Riders in a group react to each other, not to you; their next move is impossible to predict.

choices.t: Stay close behind so you can pass at the first gap.
choices.why: At close range any fall happens right in front of you.

title: Passing a stopped bus
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. A bus has stopped at a stop on your side.
question: As you get close, what is the main danger?

choices.t: The bus pulling out — so speed up to get past.
choices.why: Speeding past a bus is exactly when a hidden pedestrian appears.

choices.t: Nothing, the bus is stopped.
choices.why: A stopped bus hides everything in front of it.

choices.t: People stepping out from in front of the bus — slow right down and pass with care.
choices.why: Passengers who just got off often cross in front of the bus, hidden until they step out.

choices.t: Oncoming traffic only.
choices.why: Check oncoming traffic too, but the hidden pedestrian is the bigger risk.

title: A bus pulling out
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. A bus at a stop ahead on your left has its right indicator on.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Speed up to get past before it moves.
choices.why: If it moves while you're alongside, it will squeeze you towards oncoming traffic.

choices.t: Sound the horn so it waits for you.
choices.why: A bus driver may not hear you, and the horn does not create space.

choices.t: Slow down and let it pull out if you safely can.
choices.why: A bus moving off is slow and big; giving way early is safer and keeps traffic flowing.

choices.t: Overtake it on the right without checking oncoming traffic.
choices.why: You'd be in the oncoming lane beside a moving bus.

title: A broken-down truck in your lane
brief: Two-lane road, 50 km/h. A truck has broken down in your lane; a car is coming the other way.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Slow down and wait behind the truck until the oncoming car has passed, then go round it.
choices.why: The oncoming car has priority because the obstruction is on your side.

choices.t: Pull out now — the oncoming car will slow for you.
choices.why: It may not, and you'd meet head-on beside the truck.

choices.t: Flash your lights and pull out.
choices.why: Flashing doesn't give you the right of way.

choices.t: Drive onto the left shoulder at speed to pass.
choices.why: The shoulder may be soft or hide people working on the truck.

title: A truck turning left
brief: Town junction, 20 km/h. A long truck ahead is turning left into the side road and swings out to the right first.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Pass on the left while it swings right.
choices.why: As it turns, the trailer sweeps over exactly that space.

choices.t: Pass on the right because it is going left.
choices.why: It may need part of your lane to complete the turn.

choices.t: Stay well back and don't try to pass on either side until it has completed the turn.
choices.why: Long vehicles swing wide and their rear wheels cut in; the space beside them disappears.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep moving.
choices.why: The driver can't make the truck turn any tighter.

title: A bus on a hairpin bend
brief: Ghat road, 30 km/h, climbing a tight hairpin. A bus is coming down and cutting across the centre.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Slow down, keep left and stop if needed to let it round the bend.
choices.why: Large vehicles need the whole road on hairpins; going uphill you can stop and restart more easily.

choices.t: Keep to the centre so it has to stay on its side.
choices.why: There is no room for it to do that; you'd meet head-on.

choices.t: Speed up to get round the bend first.
choices.why: You'd meet the bus mid-bend at a higher speed.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep going.
choices.why: Sounding the horn before a blind bend is useful; it doesn't replace giving way.

title: A private bus overtaking you
brief: Two-lane road, 50 km/h. A private bus behind is overtaking close as it races to the next stop.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Speed up so it can't get in front.
choices.why: Racing a bus side by side leaves neither of you room.

choices.t: Ease off, keep left and let it pass — then keep your distance.
choices.why: Matching or blocking a racing bus turns a nuisance into a crash risk.

choices.t: Brake hard so it has to pull back.
choices.why: A sudden stop may cause a crash behind or beside you.

choices.t: Move to the centre to stop it passing.
choices.why: It's already alongside; moving right pushes into it.

title: A motorcycle hidden by a truck
brief: Town road, 20 km/h. You want to turn right into a petrol station; an oncoming truck has stopped to let you across.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Turn quickly — the truck driver has waved you through.
choices.why: The truck driver can't see that lane for you.

choices.t: Turn normally; the road beyond the truck is clear.
choices.why: You can't see past the truck to know that.

choices.t: Sound the horn and turn.
choices.why: A rider at speed won't have time to react.

choices.t: Edge forward slowly and look past the truck — a motorcycle may be overtaking it.
choices.why: A courteous wave doesn't clear the lane beside the truck, where a bike can be hidden.

title: A scooter at a side road
brief: Main road, 40 km/h. A scooter is coming fast up the side road on your left.
question: It doesn't look like slowing. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep your speed; you're on the main road.
choices.why: Priority doesn't protect you from someone who doesn't stop.

choices.t: Speed up to pass before it arrives.
choices.why: You'd reach the junction at the same moment, faster.

choices.t: Ease off and cover the brake — be ready for it to pull out.
choices.why: You have priority, but a rider going too fast to stop will come out anyway.

choices.t: Swerve into the oncoming lane early.
choices.why: You might meet oncoming traffic for a hazard that may not happen.

title: Moving off at a green light
brief: Signal junction. Your light has just turned green.
question: A car is approaching fast from the left. What do you do?

choices.t: Move off immediately — it's your green.
choices.why: A driver rushing the red won't stop for your green.

choices.t: Sound the horn and move off.
choices.why: The other driver may not hear or react in time.

choices.t: Wait and look both ways before moving — that car may run the red.
choices.why: Green means you may go if the way is clear, not that it is clear.

choices.t: Move off quickly to clear the junction before it arrives.
choices.why: You'd be in the middle of the junction when it arrives.

title: The light turns amber
brief: Signal junction, 50 km/h. The light turns amber just before the stop line; a car is close behind you.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Stop if you can do so safely; go on only if you're too close to stop.
choices.why: Amber means stop unless stopping would be unsafe. A tailgater is a reason to brake early and smoothly, not to race.

choices.t: Speed up to beat the red.
choices.why: Pedestrians and cross traffic start moving as the light changes.

choices.t: Brake as hard as possible.
choices.why: A sudden stop with a car close behind risks a rear-end crash.

choices.t: Keep the same speed and decide at the line.
choices.why: Waiting leaves you too close to stop safely.

title: A side road hidden by a parked truck
brief: Main road, 40 km/h. A truck is parked just before a side road on your left, hiding it from view.
question: A car's bonnet appears past the truck. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep your speed — you have priority on the main road.
choices.why: Priority doesn't help if the other driver can't see you.

choices.t: Speed up to pass the junction before it comes out.
choices.why: You'd arrive faster just as it nudges out.

choices.t: Slow down, move out a little if it's clear and be ready to stop — the driver can't see you either.
choices.why: A blocked view works both ways; the emerging driver may pull out blind.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep going at the same speed.
choices.why: The horn may help, but only slowing gives you time to stop.

title: An ambulance behind you
brief: Four-lane road, 60 km/h. An ambulance with lights and siren is coming up behind you in your lane.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Brake hard and stop where you are.
choices.why: Stopping in its lane blocks it and risks being hit from behind.

choices.t: Speed up to stay ahead of it.
choices.why: That doesn't clear its path and makes you a hazard at speed.

choices.t: Check mirrors, signal and move out of its path smoothly when it's safe, then let it pass.
choices.why: Make room calmly and predictably; a sudden stop or swerve can cause another crash.

choices.t: Follow closely behind it after it passes.
choices.why: It may brake suddenly; slipstreaming an ambulance is dangerous.

title: A car close behind you
brief: Four-lane road, 70 km/h. A car is driving very close behind you.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Tap the brakes to warn it.
choices.why: Brake-checking can cause the very crash you fear.

choices.t: Increase the gap ahead of you so you can brake gently, and let it pass if you can.
choices.why: More space in front means you won't need to brake hard, which protects you from the car behind.

choices.t: Speed up to get away.
choices.why: It will likely follow, and you'll both be going faster with no gap.

choices.t: Ignore it and keep the same gap ahead.
choices.why: If you brake hard, the car behind can't stop in time.

title: Overtaking a lorry before a crest
brief: Two-lane road, 50 km/h, behind a slow lorry. The road rises to a crest ahead.
question: A car appears over the crest. Should you overtake?

choices.t: Yes — go now before the car gets closer.
choices.why: You'd be alongside the lorry when you meet it.

choices.t: Yes, if you flash your lights first.
choices.why: Flashing doesn't make room on a two-lane road.

choices.t: Pull out halfway to look.
choices.why: Half out puts you in the oncoming car's path.

choices.t: No — stay behind until you can see a long, clear stretch.
choices.why: Over a crest you can't see what's coming; here a car appeared just as you'd be alongside the lorry.

title: An oncoming car overtaking towards you
brief: Two-lane road, 60 km/h. An oncoming car pulls out to overtake a truck and is coming into your lane.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Brake firmly and move left to give it room.
choices.why: Reducing the closing speed and making space is the only way to avoid a head-on crash.

choices.t: Hold your line and flash — it's in your lane.
choices.why: Being in the right won't make the impact any less.

choices.t: Swerve right into its lane.
choices.why: It may pull back in at the same moment.

choices.t: Speed up to pass the truck before it gets there.
choices.why: Higher closing speed makes any collision far worse.

title: A car joining from a slip road
brief: Four-lane highway, 70 km/h, left lane. A car is joining from a slip road on your left.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Keep your speed — joining traffic must give way.
choices.why: It should, but it may not have room to stop on a short slip road.

choices.t: Check mirrors and move right if it's clear, or adjust speed so it can merge.
choices.why: Helping traffic merge keeps everyone moving and avoids a squeeze.

choices.t: Speed up to close the gap.
choices.why: You'd force it to stop at the end of the slip road or squeeze in.

choices.t: Brake hard to let it in.
choices.why: A sudden stop on a highway invites a rear-end crash.

title: Traffic stopped ahead
brief: Highway, 80 km/h. Over a bend, traffic ahead has stopped in a queue.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Brake at the last moment to keep your place.
choices.why: Late braking leaves no margin and surprises drivers behind.

choices.t: Swerve onto the shoulder to get past the queue.
choices.why: The shoulder may be blocked or have people on it.

choices.t: Brake early and firmly, and switch on hazard lights to warn drivers behind.
choices.why: Stopping early leaves room and the flashing lights warn the traffic behind you.

choices.t: Change lanes to the one that is moving.
choices.why: Every lane ahead has stopped.

title: A car driving the wrong way
brief: Divided highway, 70 km/h, left lane. A car is coming towards you in the right lane of your carriageway.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Slow down, stay in the left lane and keep well clear; warn others with lights if safe.
choices.why: The wrong-way driver may weave; keeping to the far side and slowing gives you the most room.

choices.t: Move to the right lane to block it.
choices.why: You'd put yourself directly in its path.

choices.t: Stop in the lane and wait.
choices.why: Traffic behind may not stop, and the car may still come your way.

choices.t: Speed up to get past it quickly.
choices.why: A head-on at higher speed is far more dangerous.

title: A pedestrian in dark clothes
brief: Unlit road at night, 50 km/h. Someone in dark clothes is walking on the road edge in your direction.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Switch to high beam and keep your speed.
choices.why: High beam helps you see but doesn't give you more stopping room.

choices.t: Sound the horn as you pass.
choices.why: It can startle them into stepping the wrong way.

choices.t: Pass close; they're walking away from you.
choices.why: They can't see you and may step out round a puddle or pothole.

choices.t: Slow down and give plenty of room as you pass.
choices.why: Pedestrians in dark clothes are seen late; you need extra margin.

title: Dazzled by oncoming lights
brief: Night, 50 km/h. An oncoming car has its high beam on and you're dazzled; there's a cyclist with no light near your side.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Put your own high beam on to dazzle them back.
choices.why: Two dazzled drivers is worse than one.

choices.t: Keep your speed and look at the lights.
choices.why: Looking into the lights makes the dazzle worse and you're driving blind.

choices.t: Close your eyes for a moment until it passes.
choices.why: Even a second without seeing at speed covers many metres.

choices.t: Slow down, look towards the left edge of the road and be ready to stop.
choices.why: When dazzled you can't see what's in your lane — like this unlit cyclist.

title: The car ahead brakes in rain
brief: Heavy rain, 50 km/h. The car ahead suddenly brakes.
question: What should you have done already, and what now?

choices.t: Kept the normal gap — now brake as hard as possible.
choices.why: Harsh braking on water risks a skid, and a normal gap is too short.

choices.t: Kept close to see its brake lights — now swerve.
choices.why: Swerving on a wet road can make you lose control.

choices.t: Nothing — ABS will stop you in the same distance.
choices.why: ABS helps you steer; it doesn't shorten wet stopping distance much.

choices.t: Kept at least double the dry-weather gap — now brake smoothly and firmly.
choices.why: Wet roads can double stopping distances; a bigger gap lets you brake without skidding.

title: A slow vehicle in fog
brief: Thick fog, 50 km/h. A slow tractor with weak lights appears ahead in your lane.
question: What should your speed have been?

choices.t: Slow enough to stop within the distance you can see — now brake and follow at a safe gap.
choices.why: In fog you must be able to stop within what you can see; slow vehicles appear suddenly.

choices.t: Normal speed with high beam on.
choices.why: High beam reflects off fog and makes it harder to see.

choices.t: Close behind other cars to follow their lights.
choices.why: You'd have no room to stop if they braked.

choices.t: Fast, to get out of the fog sooner.
choices.why: Speed in fog leaves no time to react.

title: A pedestrian under an umbrella
brief: Rain, town road, 40 km/h, approaching a crossing. A woman holds an umbrella low over her head.
question: She steps towards the crossing. What do you do?

choices.t: Keep going — she'll see you and wait.
choices.why: She may not see you at all under the umbrella.

choices.t: Sound the horn to warn her.
choices.why: She may step back or forward unpredictably.

choices.t: Slow down early and be ready to stop — her umbrella blocks her view of you.
choices.why: Umbrellas and rain hoods hide traffic from pedestrians, and wet roads need longer to stop.

choices.t: Brake hard only when she steps onto the road.
choices.why: On a wet road that may be too late.

title: A dog at the roadside
brief: Village road, 50 km/h. A dog is sniffing at the edge and looks up as you approach.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Swerve hard if it runs out.
choices.why: A sudden swerve can put you off the road or into oncoming traffic.

choices.t: Slow down and be ready to stop — it may run across without warning.
choices.why: Animals don't judge traffic; slowing early is safer than a late swerve.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep your speed.
choices.why: The horn can make a dog bolt in any direction, including towards you.

choices.t: Keep going; it's on the edge.
choices.why: It can be in front of you in a moment.

title: Cattle being herded
brief: Rural road, 40 km/h. A herder is moving cattle along the road towards you.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Sound the horn to move the cattle aside.
choices.why: Startled cattle can charge or scatter into your path.

choices.t: Drive slowly through the middle of the herd.
choices.why: An animal may turn into the car without warning.

choices.t: Slow right down or stop, and wait for the herder to clear a way.
choices.why: Cattle startle easily and move unpredictably; the herder knows how to move them safely.

choices.t: Turn on your headlights and drive on.
choices.why: Lights don't move cattle and may unsettle them.

title: A cyclist from a village lane
brief: Rural road, 50 km/h. A cyclist is rolling down a lane on your left without slowing.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Keep going — the cyclist has to give way.
choices.why: They may not be able to, or may not look.

choices.t: Slow down and be ready to stop — the cyclist may roll straight out.
choices.why: Cyclists on lanes often don't stop at the main road, and may have weak brakes.

choices.t: Sound the horn and keep your speed.
choices.why: The cyclist may not be able to stop even if they hear you.

choices.t: Swerve towards the centre now.
choices.why: You may need that space for oncoming traffic, and the cyclist may still come out.

title: A slow tractor ahead
brief: Rural road, 30 km/h behind a slow tractor. There's a field entrance on the left; its indicator isn't working.
question: You want to overtake. What do you do?

choices.t: Wait — it may turn left or right at the entrance; overtake only once it's clear what it's doing.
choices.why: Farm vehicles often turn into fields without signals and may swing out first.

choices.t: Overtake now on the right.
choices.why: If it swings out right to turn left, you'll be hit.

choices.t: Overtake on the left.
choices.why: It may be turning left into exactly that space.

choices.t: Sound the horn and overtake.
choices.why: The driver may not hear over the engine.

title: A parked car pulling out
brief: Town road, 40 km/h. A parked car ahead has its wheels turned out and exhaust smoke showing.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Speed up to pass before it moves.
choices.why: If it pulls out as you arrive, there's no time to stop.

choices.t: Keep your speed — parked cars must wait.
choices.why: They should, but the driver may not have seen you.

choices.t: Slow down and be ready for it to pull out in front of you.
choices.why: Turned wheels, exhaust and a driver inside are all clues it's about to move.

choices.t: Move into the oncoming lane early without checking.
choices.why: You're swapping one hazard for a bigger one.

title: A car reversing out of a gate
brief: Residential road, 30 km/h. A car is reversing out of a house gate on your left.
question: What do you do?

choices.t: Sound the horn and drive past quickly.
choices.why: The driver may keep reversing into your path.

choices.t: Keep going — it must wait for you.
choices.why: It should, but it may not have seen you.

choices.t: Slow down or stop and let it finish — the driver's view behind is poor.
choices.why: Reversing drivers see little; giving them time avoids a collision.

choices.t: Pass on the right without checking oncoming traffic.
choices.why: You'd trade one risk for a head-on one.
